title: The Long Clock
premise: In the river town of Saint-Aubin, 1848, Coral Joubert has survived by making herself small: cutting type by day, memorizing which neighbors vanish in the night, and saying nothing. When her father's press is seized for printing seditious pamphlets he never set, and the winter bridge closes with him imprisoned across the river, Coral inherits both his trade and his danger. She discovers the true evidence of his innocence hidden inside a font of type he cast for her years ago, and must carry it past three checkpoints before the spring thaw reopens the river and the tribunal convenes. The book ends with Coral choosing to testify openly rather than stay invisible, trading her safety for justice and finally claiming her own name.
about_author: P. M. Whitlock is the pen name of a former letterpress apprentice who spent a decade restoring nineteenth-century print shops before turning to fiction. They write historical novels about ordinary people caught in machinery larger than themselves.

chapters.title: The Weight of Letters
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. Establishes the print shop, her father Auguste's arrest during a midnight raid, and the town's careful silence. Coral burns nothing and says nothing, learning the charges hinge on pamphlets she knows he never printed. Emotional beat: numb shock hardening into resolve as she realizes no one will speak for him.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. The bridge closes for the season; the tribunal sits on the far bank in spring. She sorts her father's type cases looking for anything useful and finds one font heavier than it should be, each sort stamped with tiny marks she doesn't recognize. Emotional beat: grief interrupted by the first spark of hope.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Coral's POV, with an interlude from gendarme Captain Roche. She maps the route: the mill gate, the customs house, the ferry landing, each guarded by men with their own debts and fears. Roche, ambitious and watchful, suspects the Joubert household but lacks proof. Emotional beat: dread tempered by the discovery that power is made of cracks.

chapters.title: The Widow Vasseur
chapters.summary: Coral's POV. She seeks help from a neighbor who once informed on her own husband to survive, hoping she'll understand. The widow refuses to act but teaches Coral how informants think, and where the mill gate's ledger lies. Emotional beat: bitter kinship between two women shaped by the same fear.

chapters.title: A Font of Evidence
chapters.summary: Coral deciphers the marks: each stamped sort records dates and names proving the seized pamphlets were printed elsewhere, by the magistrate's own cousin. She begins casting duplicates, hiding them in candle stubs and bread loaves. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into purpose; her craft becomes her weapon.

chapters.title: The Mill Gate
chapters.summary: First checkpoint. Coral carries loaves through the mill gate while Roche watches, and nearly loses everything when a guard weighs her basket. A miller's boy covers for her out of old kindness to her father. Emotional beat: the cost of other people's courage, and guilt at accepting it.

chapters.title: Roche's Bargain
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Roche confronts Coral privately, revealing he knows more than he lets on — and offers to look away if she gives him the magistrate's cousin instead of the magistrate. Coral must decide whether justice served by a self-serving man is still justice. Emotional beat: moral vertigo; the law and the truth are not the same thing.

chapters.title: The Customs House Fire
chapters.summary: Second checkpoint goes wrong: the duplicate types are destroyed when the customs house burns — set, Coral realizes, by someone protecting the cousin. Her originals survive only because she kept one back out of superstition. Emotional beat: despair, then fury that clarifies rather than paralyzes.

chapters.title: Before the Ice Breaks
chapters.summary: Climax. At the ferry landing, Coral walks past the third checkpoint carrying the last sort openly, daring the guards to stop a woman delivering type to the tribunal itself. Roche holds the crowd back with a technicality. The ice groans and breaks behind her as she crosses. Emotional beat: transcendence — invisibility abandoned at last.

chapters.title: Her Own Name
chapters.summary: Resolution. At the tribunal, Coral testifies, naming herself as the daughter who read the type. Her father is freed; the cousin flees; Roche takes quiet credit and Coral lets him, knowing the difference between winning and being seen to win. She reopens the shop under her own name. Emotional beat: hard-won peace — survival was the price, identity the reward.
